content: Bullous pemphigoid (BP) is the most common autoimmune blistering disease, and oral steroids are the standard treatment. This review, originally published in 2002, has been updated to include new treatments that have been trialed since then. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of various treatments for BP. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of treatments for BP confirmed by immunofluorescence. The primary outcomes assessed were the healing of skin lesions and mortality. A total of 14 RCTs involving 1,442 participants were identified. The main treatments studied were oral steroids, topical steroids, and the oral anti-inflammatory antibiotic doxycycline. Most studies reported mortality, but adverse events and quality of life were not well-documented. The results were based on single studies for most comparisons, except for azathioprine. Many studies had small sample sizes and were assessed as having a high risk of bias or some concerns due to missing data, inappropriate analysis, or insufficient information. Clobetasol Propionate Cream vs. Oral Prednisone Clobetasol propionate cream applied over the whole body likely increases skin healing at day 21 compared to oral prednisone (99.8% vs. 92.4% of participants, respectively). This is supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Clobetasol propionate cream may reduce mortality at one year compared to oral prednisone (26.5% vs. 36.3%, respectively), but the evidence is of low certainty. Clobetasol propionate cream may reduce the risk of severe complications by day 21 compared to oral prednisone, based on low-certainty evidence. Quality of life was not measured in this study. Mild vs. Standard Regimen of Clobetasol Propionate Cream A mild regimen of clobetasol propionate cream (10-30 g/day) compared to the standard regimen (40 g/day) likely does not change skin healing at day 21, with both groups achieving complete healing in 98% of participants. This is supported by moderate-certainty evidence. Mortality at one year was similar between the mild and standard regimens (37.9% in both groups), but the evidence is of low certainty. Adverse events at one year were also similar between the two regimens, based on low-certainty evidence. Quality of life was not measured in this study. Doxycycline vs. Prednisolone Doxycycline (200 mg/day) is less effective than prednisolone (0.5 mg/kg/day) in inducing skin healing at six weeks (73.8% vs. 91.1%, respectively). This is supported by high-certainty evidence. Doxycycline likely reduces mortality at one year compared to prednisolone (2.3% vs. 9.1%, respectively), with moderate-certainty evidence. Doxycycline improved quality of life at one year compared to prednisolone, as measured by the Dermatology Life Quality Index (mean difference of 1.8 points lower, favoring doxycycline). This is supported by high-certainty evidence. Doxycycline likely reduces severe or life-threatening treatment-related adverse events at one year compared to prednisolone, based on moderate-certainty evidence. Prednisone Plus Azathioprine vs. Prednisone Alone It is unclear whether the combination of azathioprine and prednisone compared to prednisone alone affects skin healing or mortality due to very low-certainty evidence from two trials involving 98 participants. Adverse events were reported in 42% of participants in the azathioprine plus prednisone group and 34% in the prednisone-alone group. Quality of life was not measured in these studies. Nicotinamide Plus Tetracycline vs. Prednisone It is unclear whether nicotinamide plus tetracycline compared to prednisone affects skin healing or mortality due to very low-certainty evidence from one trial involving 18 participants. Fewer adverse events were reported in the nicotinamide group. Quality of life was not measured in this study. Methylprednisolone Plus Azathioprine vs. Methylprednisolone Plus Dapsone It is unclear whether azathioprine plus methylprednisolone compared to dapsone plus methylprednisolone affects skin healing or mortality due to very low-certainty evidence from one trial involving 54 participants. A total of 18 adverse events were reported in the azathioprine group, compared to 13 in the dapsone group. Quality of life was not measured in this study. Authors' Conclusions Clobetasol propionate cream applied over the whole body is likely as effective as oral prednisone for treating BP and may result in lower mortality. Lower-dose clobetasol propionate cream is likely as effective as the standard dose and has similar mortality. Doxycycline is less effective than prednisolone for skin healing but is associated with lower mortality and better quality of life. Other treatments, such as azathioprine, nicotinamide, tetracycline, and dapsone, require further investigation due to insufficient evidence.
